result: The authors determined a 3.9 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 complex, representing the first structure of a membrane protein and non-kinase client of the Hsp90–Cdc37 system. The complex is a hetero-tetramer with one GC-C monomer bound to an Hsp90 dimer and one Cdc37, with the GC-C client unfolded into the Hsp90 channel and Hsp90 in a canonical closed conformation.
evaluation: Claims C3, C32-C34 are directly supported by the cryo-EM data (3.9 Å resolution, structural composition, Hsp90 conformation). Claims C35-C36 regarding novelty are supported by comparison with existing literature. Claims C37-C40 describe validated methodological approaches. Claims C41-C43 are reasonable inferences from the structural data about the absence of density for the second GC-C monomer and functional implications.

result: The structure reveals that Cdc37 mediates GC-C recruitment by displacing the N-lobe of the pseudokinase domain, binding to the C-lobe at the N-C interface (689 Å² interface), and guiding the unfolded N-lobe (residues 528-544) into the Hsp90 dimer channel. The interface is driven by charge complementarity (arginine cluster R30, R32, R39 on Cdc37 interacting with D609, Y580, T586 on GC-C) and shape complementarity.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2. Claims C47-C49 provide quantitative measurements from the structure with appropriate citation of the calculation method (PISA). Claims C50-C53 are reasonable inferences from the structural analysis regarding interface properties and density quality, consistent with the reported resolution and mobility of unfolded regions.

result: Structural comparison with other client–Hsp90–Cdc37 complexes (Cdk4, RAF1, B-raf) reveals conserved Cdc37-mediated recruitment mechanisms despite significant sequence divergence. GC-C shows 19-25% identity and 31-41% homology with other kinase clients, yet Hsp90–Cdc37 shows high structural conservation (Cα RMSDs 1.4-3.3 Å for Hsp90, 1.5-2.5 Å for Cdc37), demonstrating that Cdc37 serves as a central binding platform relatively independent of sequence identity.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by structural comparisons with cited structures and quantitative RMSD measurements. Claims C57-C58 are supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C. Claims C59-C61 are well-supported inferences from the structural conservation data and comparisons with kinase clients, demonstrating the mechanistic conservation despite sequence divergence.

result: The authors propose that pseudokinase domains of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases have evolved to hijack kinase regulatory mechanisms, fitting a model where ligand-induced activity destabilizes the PK domain, facilitating Hsp90–Cdc37 binding for refolding and continued catalysis. This is supported by previous work showing geldanamycin (Hsp90 inhibitor) reduces cGMP output and Hsp90-GC-A association.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 cite a previously proposed model (Taipale et al., 2012) which is appropriate context. Claim C64 is speculative inference about evolutionary function. Claims C65-C67 reference prior work (Kumar et al., 2001) but the mechanistic model proposed is largely speculative and not directly tested in this study. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation beyond the structural data presented.

result: The authors propose three potential regulatory outcomes following Hsp90–Cdc37 complex formation: (i) refolding to maintain receptor activity, (ii) recruitment of PP5 phosphatase for dephosphorylation and activity modulation, or (iii) recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases leading to receptor removal. PP5 is known to interact with Hsp90–Cdc37 and dephosphorylate kinase clients, though its role with mGCs remains uncertain.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 cite established knowledge about PP5 with appropriate references, though C69 notes conflicting evidence about PP5-mGC interaction. Claims C70-C74 are explicitly speculative scenarios ("could") shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, representing hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. These are reasonable mechanistic proposals based on known Hsp90 biology, but lack direct experimental support in this study and require future validation.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases, cGMP signaling, domain architecture, and regulation through phosphorylation and Hsp90–Cdc37 association, establishing the physiological and structural context for the study.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C20 establish the physiological roles of mGCs and cGMP with appropriate citations. Claims C21-C27 describe the established domain architecture of mGCs with citations. Claims C28-C31 describe known regulatory mechanisms with appropriate citations. These are well-established background claims from the literature that provide context for the current work.

result: The authors describe detailed methods for construct design (leucine zipper replacing ECD, residues 399-1053 of GC-C), protein expression in ExpiCHO cells, purification using FLAG affinity chromatography with DDM/CHS detergents, cryo-EM grid preparation and data collection on a 200 kV Glacios microscope, and image processing yielding 165,635 particles with a final model having favorable validation statistics (MolProbity score 2.14, 0.4% Ramachandran outliers).
evaluation: Claims C75-C88 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and follow standard practices for cryo-EM structure determination. The construct design (C75-C76) is well-justified with citation. Expression and purification methods (C77-C80) are standard and appropriately detailed. Cryo-EM data collection parameters (C81-C84) and processing workflow (C85-C87) are clearly described. Model validation statistics (C88) indicate good quality structure. All methods claims are supported by the data and appropriate citations.

result: The work demonstrates that GC-C is a membrane protein and non-kinase client of Hsp90–Cdc37, showing how membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases hijack regulatory mechanisms used for active kinases.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are directly demonstrated by the structural data showing GC-C (a membrane protein with a pseudokinase domain) in complex with Hsp90–Cdc37. Claim C6 is supported by structural comparisons with kinase–Hsp90–Cdc37 complexes showing conserved mechanisms despite GC-C being a non-kinase. The term "hijack" is interpretive but reasonable given the structural and mechanistic conservation.
